newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU agrees measures to fight child sex trade.
newsitem.headline: EU agrees measures to fight child sex trade.

text.p: European Union justice ministers, reacting to a Belgian child-murder and sex scandal, on Thursday agreed to extend the scope of the EU's police agency Europol so it could help fight the sex trade in children and women.

Irish Justice Minister Nora Owen said the ministers, meeting for a two-day session in Dublin, reached political agreement on the plan to extend the mandate of the Europol Drugs Unit to cover this kind of crime.

"We intend to fight against the work of criminals in the trafficking of people in the same way as we fight against drugs trafficking," Chief of the Hague-based agency Juergen Storbeck told reporters after the agreement was made.
The agreement, which includes a move to exchange police officers throughout the EU and set up centres to fight the sex trade will be formalised at another meeting of EU ministers.

EU members, traditionally reluctant to increase the EU's crime-fighting role, were stung into action after the discovery of the bodies of four murdered girls in Belgium highlighted the world trade in child sex and pornography.
"I'm very impressed. In the 20 years I've been in the business I've never seen such speed of agreement," Storbeck said.

Storbeck said the agency, which already helps fight drugs trafficking and money laundering, could help speed up exchanges of information between different police bureaux in the 15-nation EU and carry out strategic analysis.
With Europol's help information on missing children and people suspected of abducting them could be exchanged between criminal, customs and border police in less than an hour.
The agency could help coordinate parallel investigations in different member states, he said.
Over the next few weeks Europol officers would meet to try and identify problems in international cooperation and develop new methods of fighting the crime.
"This will lead to a common action plan to be given to ministers for possible agreement this year or the beginning of next year," he said.
But Storbeck urged ministers to ratify the Europol convention urgently so the agency could pool and analyse information via its central computer.
He stressed the agency, which employs 115 officials, could not instigate and carry out investigations on its own, but could only back up work done by national police agencies.
"We are only a support unit and if they request support we give that support," he said, adding it was not yet clear exactly how many new staff Europol might need to carry out its new role.
